transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I... I suppose I'm here because I just don't know what else to do anymore. It's really hard to explain, but most days I feel like I’m just sitting at the bottom of a dark hole. And I mean a really deep, pitch-black hole where you can't even see the top. I've been doing maintenance and repair work for years, you know, ever since I got out of high school, and usually I'm out on job sites, working with my hands, talking to the same crew I've known forever. But lately... well, even when I’m right there around people I know, people I've worked with for over a decade, I just can’t shake this heavy, hopeless feeling. 

It's like I'm not really there with them. I'm just down in that hole, and it's so heavy. I try to put on a brave face while I'm fixing a unit or talking to a customer, but the hopelessness just sits on me like a physical weight, and I can't get rid of it no matter how hard I try to just act normal. I keep thinking if I just keep busy it'll pass, but it doesn't. It doesn't matter who is around me or how sunny it is outside, that heavy feeling is just always there, pulling me down, making it feel like it takes a hundred pounds of effort just to stand there.
How long have you been feeling this way? Can you pinpoint when these feelings of heaviness and hopelessness started?

Well, if I really think about it... yeah, I can pinpoint it exactly, actually. It’s been... gosh, right about a year and two months now. A year and two months of just... dragging myself through this. 

It all started with this one specific job. We were out doing a commercial HVAC install—one of those massive rooftop units, you know? The ones where you have to haul all your heavy gear up the side access and you're just baking in the sun. We were trying to get it done before the weather turned, just rushing a little bit I guess, and... well, I had a fall. I just lost my footing. It wasn't even the highest drop I've ever had, but I landed so wrong, and it left me with this terrible back injury. 

And, you know, when you've been doing physical labor, working with your hands and relying on your back since you were eighteen right out of high school, an injury like that... it just changes everything. That was the exact moment everything started unraveling. I mean, my whole life just started coming apart at the seams after that fall. First it was just trying to deal with the physical part of it, being stuck sitting at home, worrying about my crew and my paycheck, and then... then it was like that dark hole I was telling you about just opened up right underneath me. I just kept sinking, and I haven't been able to climb out since. So, yeah, fourteen months. Ever since that stupid HVAC job.
Since the injury, have you noticed that things you used to enjoy, like your work or time with your crew, don’t bring you the same satisfaction anymore?

Yeah, work and the crew... but honestly, it's not just the job. It's literally everything. I mean, I used to get a real kick out of a tricky install. You know, when the blueprints don't quite match the reality of the building and you have to really use your brain and your hands to figure out how to route the ductwork, or when you have to fix a busted compressor that everyone else gave up on? I used to love that challenge. It felt so good to solve it. 

But it's not just the work stuff I've lost. It bleeds into all my off-the-clock time, too. I used to be so active and into so many different things. I loved hiking. I'd go up to the trails every other weekend, just putting miles on my boots and clearing my head. And when I wasn't doing that, I was painting. Watercolors, mostly, just landscapes and things. Or I'd be down at the local makerspace. Have you ever been to one of those? It's this great community workshop where you can just tinker and build things. I had this whole project going where I was restoring this old antique desk fan, stripping the metal, rewiring the whole motor... 

But now... I don't even know. My painting stuff is just sitting right there on the kitchen table. The brushes, the tubes of paint, the heavy paper... it's just gathering dust. I literally just sit there in a chair and stare at the supplies. I look at them and I think, "I should paint, I used to like this," but the thought of actually picking up a brush just feels... impossible. Like, what's the point? It doesn't feel worth starting. None of it does. 

And the people... my crew, the folks from the makerspace, my hiking buddies... they try to reach out. My phone will ring, and I'll see the caller ID, and I know it's them wanting to see how I'm doing or asking if I want to come hang out, and I just... I just watch the screen light up. I ignore the calls. I let them all go to voicemail because I can't muster the energy to talk, and I don't want to explain that I just don't care about any of it anymore. It's just so exhausting to even think about doing any of the things that used to make me, well, me. It’s like the spark is just completely dead. I just keep staring at that stupid half-finished antique fan in my living room, and I can't bring myself to even pick up a screwdriver.

Have there been times in the past—before this injury and the feelings you described—when you felt down or hopeless for a period of time, or has this been something completely different and new compared to how you've felt in the past?

Well, no, not really. I mean, sure, I've had bad days. Everyone has bad days, right? Like when I was in my twenties, maybe twenty-five or twenty-six, I went through this really nasty breakup with this guy I thought I was going to marry. We had this whole life planned out, and when it fell apart, I was pretty devastated for a few weeks. I remember I ate a lot of ice cream and watched a bunch of sad movies, and I cried on my best friend's couch for a solid weekend. But even then, even when I was heartbroken, I still went to work. I still cared if my tools were clean and organized. I still wanted to go out and hike on the weekends, even if I was a little sad while I was doing it. 

And there was that time, maybe eight or nine years ago, when the company I was working for went under. We all lost our jobs right before the holidays. That was stressful. I mean, really stressful. I was losing sleep, worrying about how I was going to pay rent and keep the lights on. I felt anxious and down about the situation, but it wasn't this... this heavy, suffocating thing. It was just a normal reaction to a bad situation, you know? I hustled, I put my resume out there, I called every contact I had in the union, and within a month, I was back on a crew. I had the drive to fix it. 

But this... what I'm feeling now? Since that fall off the roof? No, this is completely different. This is new. It’s not just being sad or stressed out. It’s like someone reached inside me and just flipped the power switch to "off." Before the injury, I was always the one organizing the weekend hikes, always the one bringing donuts to the job site on Fridays, always the one who had a million projects going on at once. I was tired sometimes, sure, because it's hard work, but I was never... empty. This feeling of just being completely hollowed out, where even breathing feels like a chore, where I can't even look at my watercolor paints without feeling overwhelmed... no, I've never experienced anything even close to this before. It's like I'm a completely different person now, and I don't know how to get the old me back.

Have you ever experienced a time where your mood was extremely high, you felt unusually energetic, or you were doing or saying things more quickly than usual, where others might have noticed a change in you?

High? Like... unusually energetic? No. No, definitely not. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, before all this happened, I had energy. You have to have energy in my line of work, right? You can't be hauling heavy tools and ductwork up three flights of stairs or climbing extension ladders if you're dragging your feet. But it was never like... a weird energy, you know? It wasn't like I was bouncing off the walls or talking a mile a minute or anything like that. 

I remember this one time, gosh, maybe four years ago, we had this massive winter storm coming in. We were doing a rush job on a commercial boiler system for this big office park down on 4th street, and we pulled... it must have been a fourteen-hour shift, maybe fifteen. We were moving fast, yeah, because the temperature was dropping fast and the general contractor was just breathing down our necks the whole time. So I was barking orders, moving quick, telling the apprentices to hurry up with the wrenches and the sealant, just really pushing the pace. But that was just the job. That was just me trying to beat the clock before the pipes froze and caused thousands of dollars in damage. 

It wasn't some kind of... mood thing. I wasn't high on life or anything. When I got home that night, I was completely dead on my feet. I think I just ate a cold turkey sandwich standing over the sink and practically passed out with my boots still on. 

So, no, I've never had a time where I was just wired for no reason, or talking so fast people couldn't understand me, or doing things that made people look at me funny. People have always told me I'm pretty steady. Level-headed, you know? I'm usually the one who keeps everyone else calm when a pipe bursts or the wiring is totally fried and nothing matches the schematic. I've never been the type to get all frantic or overly wound up. It's always just been steady, reliable, hard work. Just putting one foot in front of the other and getting the job done. Well, until the fall, anyway. Now I don't even have the energy to make a pot of coffee in the morning, let alone bounce around or talk fast.
Since this started a year and two months ago, have you experienced these feelings of depression—like the heaviness, hopelessness, and loss of interest—nearly every day?

Yeah. Every day. It’s... honestly, it’s literally every single day. I mean, like you said, it’s been going on for about a year and two months now. Exactly fourteen months and a couple of weeks, if I’m being precise. It all started right after the fall at that HVAC job. I was up on this flat roof—commercial building, doing a pretty standard check on a rooftop condenser unit—and I just lost my footing. Went down so hard, and that back injury... well, that was the start of it. That was the exact moment when everything just started unraveling. 

And since that day, I can't remember a single morning where I woke up and felt like myself. Not one. It’s every day, Monday through Sunday. I used to know what day of the week it was because of my schedule, you know? Like, Fridays were for wrapping up the big installs, Saturdays were for the makerspace or the trails. But now? A Tuesday feels exactly the same as a Saturday. It’s just this... this constant, heavy blanket over me from the second I open my eyes. Before I even try to sit up and deal with my back, the heaviness is already there in my chest. 

There are no good days anymore, no breaks from it. You’d think after a year and two months you’d get used to it, or you'd have an afternoon where the clouds part for a minute, but... no. It just doesn't let up. It’s just been fourteen solid months of waking up and feeling completely hollowed out, day in and day out, ever since my back gave out on that roof and took my whole life down with it. I just sit in my chair and watch the clock change, and it's the exact same hopeless feeling every single day.
Have there been any periods lasting at least two months since this started where you felt significantly better or like your old self, even if just for a while?

No, no... like I was just saying a second ago, there hasn't been any break in it. There definitely hasn't been a two-month stretch where I felt better. I wish there was, I really do, but... no. Not even two days, let alone two months. 

It’s just been this one long, continuous nightmare for about a year and two months now. I mean, ever since that fall at the HVAC job—when I got this back injury—that was it. That was the exact turning point where everything just started unraveling, and it hasn't stopped unraveling since. You know, sometimes my sister will call me, or one of the guys from the union will check in, and they'll ask, "Hey, are you feeling any better lately?" or "Are things looking up?" And I hate having to tell them no, but... it's the truth. I haven't had a good week, let alone two whole months of feeling like my old self. 

My old self is just... gone. The woman who could haul compressors and organize trail hikes, she disappeared the second my boots slipped on that commercial roof fourteen months ago. That back injury didn't just break my body, it just... it took everything else down with it. It’s like pulling a loose thread on a sweater, you know? One thing goes, and then the next, and the next, and before you know it, a year and two months have gone by and you haven't had a single moment where you felt okay. So, no, definitely no periods of feeling better. Just the same heavy, awful feeling, day in and day out, ever since the fall.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if there have been any symptom-free periods lasting at least two months during the course of the depressive episode, which relates to the duration and continuity of the symptoms.

patient.answer:
No, no... like I was just saying a second ago, there hasn't been any break in it. There definitely hasn't been a two-month stretch where I felt better. I wish there was, I really do, but... no. Not even two days, let alone two months. 

It’s just been this one long, continuous nightmare for about a year and two months now. I mean, ever since that fall at the HVAC job—when I got this back injury—that was it. That was the exact turning point where everything just started unraveling, and it hasn't stopped unraveling since. You know, sometimes my sister will call me, or one of the guys from the union will check in, and they'll ask, "Hey, are you feeling any better lately?" or "Are things looking up?" And I hate having to tell them no, but... it's the truth. I haven't had a good week, let alone two whole months of feeling like my old self. 

My old self is just... gone. The woman who could haul compressors and organize trail hikes, she disappeared the second my boots slipped on that commercial roof fourteen months ago. That back injury didn't just break my body, it just... it took everything else down with it. It’s like pulling a loose thread on a sweater, you know? One thing goes, and then the next, and the next, and before you know it, a year and two months have gone by and you haven't had a single moment where you felt okay. So, no, definitely no periods of feeling better. Just the same heavy, awful feeling, day in and day out, ever since the fall.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a major depressive episode that has persisted for over two years without remission, following a clear index episode that began after a significant life event (injury). The continuous nature of symptoms for over 14 months, without any significant periods of improvement lasting two months or more, supports a diagnosis of recurrent depressive disorder, current episode severe without psychotic symptoms.
